parts.note: a broad is slang for a woman, so a dame's belongs to a broad
a term is a word or expression

explanation.surface: Someone asks what name a grand lady uses for a sword.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Dame' suggests a titled lady, but here it is just slang for a woman, BROAD; her term is her WORD.
explanation.definitionFit: A broadsword is a heavy sword with a wide cutting edge.

parts.note: a brand is a trade name or label on goods

indicators.note: only the opening letter of the word yellow is wanted here

explanation.surface: A drinks label whose first colour is yellow.
explanation.definitionFit: Brandy is a distilled liquor, and spirit is the general word for strong alcoholic drink.

parts.note: in cricket a duck is a score of nothing, written as the round letter O

indicators.note: swimming suggests the letters of Loire moving about freely into a new order

explanation.surface: A bird and a duck seen swimming on the French river Loire.
explanation.walkthrough: 'swimming' rearranges the river's name; 'duck' looks like a second bird but is the cricket zero.
explanation.definitionFit: The oriole is a songbird, the golden oriole being bright yellow and black.

clue.text: Bush may go before it, lending support to cleaner newspaper

indicators.note: in a down clue the second piece sits beneath the first, holding it up

parts.note: a daily is British slang for a cleaning woman who comes in each day
the bush telegraph is an informal grapevine for spreading news, so bush can precede this word

explanation.surface: A newspaper story on a politician named Bush and a cleaner.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bush' reads like a president, but 'bush telegraph' is the rumour network. In a down entry, TELEGRAPH below DAILY 'supports' it. A DAILY is a British house cleaner.
explanation.definitionFit: The Daily Telegraph is a British national broadsheet, the paper that published this puzzle.

parts.note: went is the past tense of go, to travel
in Cockney slang 'my old Dutch' is a man's wife

explanation.surface: A couple travelling together who split the bills.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old Dutch' is London Cockney slang for a wife (from 'duchess').
explanation.definitionFit: To go Dutch is the idiom for each person paying their own share of a bill.

indicators.note: letting the word later loose frees its letters to settle in a fresh order

explanation.surface: A meat-eating animal will be released from captivity later.
explanation.definitionFit: The ratel, or honey badger, is a fierce meat-eating mammal of Africa and Asia.

clue.text: Try to see a noble fellow

explanation.surface: An attempt to catch sight of an aristocrat.
explanation.definitionFit: To look closely and with effort is to peer; a lord is a peer of the realm, and an equal is also a peer.

clue.text: College boy's attire, note, upset clubs, for example

indicators.note: in a down clue upset turns the word note upside down, so it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: the word note itself, taken as written
clubs is one example of a suit of playing cards

explanation.surface: A schoolboy's outfit, a note, and some knocked-over golf clubs.
explanation.walkthrough: 'upset' turns NOTE into ETON; 'clubs' looks like golf but is the card suit.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton College's traditional uniform of short jacket and wide collar was worn by its younger pupils.

clue.text: Booming notes ran in the wrong order

indicators.note: the letters of notes ran are set down jumbled rather than as printed

explanation.surface: Loud musical notes played out of sequence.
explanation.definitionFit: A resonant sound is deep and echoing, like a voice that booms.

clue.text: A certain Scottish girl in current novel

indicators.note: the run of A, the word for certain and the girl's name sits inside the word for current

parts.note: a trend is a current or prevailing tendency
sure means certain
Isla is a Scottish girl's name, after the island and river

explanation.surface: A Scottish girl appearing in a fashionable novel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'current' suggests up-to-date, but it means a tendency, and 'in' has it split open around the other three pieces.
explanation.definitionFit: Treasure Island is Robert Louis Stevenson's adventure novel about pirates and buried gold.

clue.text: Jumping bail, I must make an excuse

indicators.note: jumping suggests the letters of bail and I leaping into a new order

explanation.surface: A defendant who skips bail needs a good story.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Jumping bail' is a real legal phrase, but 'Jumping' is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: An alibi is a claim of being elsewhere, and more loosely any excuse.

clue.text: Having a bad name, there must be no nonsense about debts

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: about means turned round, so the word for nonsense is written backwards

parts.note: rot is nonsense
IOUs are written promises to pay debts

explanation.surface: Someone with a poor reputation is told to stop messing around with what they owe.
explanation.walkthrough: 'about' sends the word for nonsense backwards; 'there must be' is just padding linking the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Notorious means famous for something bad, so having an ill reputation.

indicators.note: during places the song within the act, so one word sits inside the other

parts.note: a deed is an act
a lay is an old word for a song or ballad

explanation.surface: A performance held up because of a song in the middle of an act.
explanation.walkthrough: 'song' is the old poetic sense, as in a minstrel's ballad; 'during' places it within the word for act.
explanation.definitionFit: Something delayed has been held up or made late, so slowed down.

clue.text: Alison I fancy for an affair

indicators.note: fancy here suggests something elaborate or decorative, so the letters are rearranged

explanation.surface: A man admits he fancies Alison and wants an affair.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fancy' reads as the verb 'desire', but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: A liaison is a secret romantic relationship, especially an adulterous one.

parts.note: a western is a classic cowboy film
the Union is a name for the United States

explanation.surface: A film studio of yesteryear based in the USA.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old film company' reads as a studio, but the definition is just 'company'; America is 'the Union'.
explanation.definitionFit: Western Union is an American firm famous for telegrams and money transfers.

clue.text: Character on form, one worthy of imitation

parts.note: a role is a character played by an actor
a model is a form or pattern to copy

explanation.surface: An actor in good form playing a part others should copy.
explanation.definitionFit: A role model is a person others look up to and copy.

indicators.note: put out suggests the letters of tureen is disturbed and set in another order

explanation.surface: A hungry diner sees the soup tureen being put out.
explanation.walkthrough: 'put out' reads as serving the dish, but it is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Esurient is a literary word meaning greedy or ravenous.

clue.text: Girl follows it up with a liqueur

indicators.note: the girl's name comes after the other pieces
in a down clue up means the word it reads from bottom to top

parts.note: the word it, taken as written
Maria is a girl's name

explanation.surface: A girl pursues something with a sweet drink.
explanation.walkthrough: 'up' reverses the word it in this down entry, and 'follows' puts the girl's name after it and the A.
explanation.definitionFit: Tia Maria is a Jamaican coffee-flavoured liqueur.

clue.text: German writer penning long story that will inspire terror

indicators.note: penning means enclosing, so the writer's name holds the other word inside it

parts.note: Friedrich Schiller was a German poet and dramatist
to pine is to long for something

explanation.surface: A German author writing a long and frightening tale.
explanation.walkthrough: 'penning' suggests writing, but here means enclosing: the dramatist's name is split after its first letter.
explanation.definitionFit: A spine-chiller is a frightening story or film that sends a shiver down the back.

explanation.surface: A firework glowing a deep reddish brown.
explanation.definitionFit: Maroon is a deep red-brown colour, and also a loud rocket used as a warning signal.

indicators.note: ringed by means surrounded, so the girl's name goes around the other word

parts.note: Ada is a girl's name
gen is British slang for information

explanation.surface: A girl surrounded by details about a schedule.
explanation.walkthrough: GEN is British slang for information, as in 'get the gen'.
explanation.definitionFit: An agenda is a list of items for a meeting, a plan or schedule.

clue.text: Contrition about son breaking in again

parts.note: re means about or concerning

indicators.note: breaking in means intruding, so the abbreviation for son forces its way into the word for again

parts.note: more can mean again, as in once more

explanation.surface: Remorse over a son who has burgled a house a second time.
explanation.walkthrough: 'breaking in' reads as burglary but means the son's abbreviation intrudes into the word for again.
explanation.definitionFit: Remorse is deep regret for wrongdoing, much the same as contrition.

indicators.note: topless means losing the top letter, which in a down entry is the first one

parts.note: to delude someone is to fool them

explanation.surface: Stay away from the idiot who appears without a shirt.
explanation.walkthrough: 'fool' looks like a noun but is the verb DELUDE, whose first letter goes.
explanation.definitionFit: To elude is to escape or dodge, so to avoid.

clue.text: Feral horse has to, nag is different

parts.note: must means has to

indicators.note: the word nag is made different by setting its letters in a new order

explanation.surface: A wild horse must be unlike an old nag.
explanation.walkthrough: 'is different' reads as a comparison of horses but signals the old nag's letters being rearranged.
explanation.definitionFit: The mustang is a free-roaming horse of the American West.

definitions.note: the 's stands for is, so the poet is what follows

parts.note: Ezra is a book of the Old Testament
twenty shillings, written 20/-, made one pound in old British money

explanation.surface: A poet's book priced at twenty shillings.
explanation.walkthrough: 20/- is pre-1971 British notation for twenty shillings, which equalled one pound.
explanation.definitionFit: Ezra Pound was an American modernist poet, author of The Cantos.

parts.note: ado is fuss or bother
RN is the Royal Navy, the sailors

explanation.surface: Trouble with crew members on board ship.
explanation.walkthrough: 'deck' looks like part of a ship, but it is the verb to decorate.
explanation.definitionFit: To deck is to decorate, as in decking the halls, which is what adorn means.

explanation.surface: Snagging a ball in a sand hazard.
explanation.definitionFit: A trap is a device for catching; on a golf course a bunker is a sand trap.

parts.note: Bella is a girl's name
Donna is a girl's name

explanation.surface: Two young women and a drug.
explanation.definitionFit: Belladonna, from deadly nightshade, yields the drug atropine.
